source.title: Does label smoothing mitigate label noise?
source.authors: Michal Lukasik; Srinadh Bhojanapalli; A. Menon; Surinder Kumar

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests training on artificially corrupted labels and reports training-set accuracy, using label-smoothing and loss-correction methods. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the finding that deep networks can fit arbitrary labels, but does not test completely random labels. Its own results test training on 20% symmetric label noise, including accuracy on the corrupted training subset.
record.test_reason: Table 3 directly measures fitting of observed corrupted training labels, bearing on V4's perfect-training-fit component at one corruption level. The study does not test completely random labeling or a corruption-rate sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that label smoothing has denoising benefits and is competitive with loss correction. They also relate smoothing to regularization and find that smoothing a teacher improves distillation under label noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses artificially injected symmetric label noise, label smoothing and loss correction; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported noisy-label training accuracy changes with the label-smoothing parameter α.

fits_no_version.finding: True-label accuracy on the corrupted training subset rises from 39.92% to 48.58% and 53.01% as smoothing increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label smoothing improves recovery of underlying true classes from partially corrupted training data.

record.problems: Only a 20% symmetric-noise condition is tested for the relevant training-set breakdown; the paper does not test completely random labels or sweep the corruption fraction. Table 3 reports no uncertainty for its accuracy values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 also reports full-training and clean-subset true-label accuracy at each α; omitted because these do not directly measure fitting the corrupted labels. Other reported test-accuracy and calibration results do not measure a version's named behavior.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error under that labeling, chance test performance, and comparison with unchanged true-label training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases. Reported runtimes provide neither comparison.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

A corruption sweep from none to all, perfect training fit throughout that sweep, and steadily increasing test error toward chance. Only the training-fit component at 20% label replacement is directly assessed.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent completely random-label fitting, and generalization after removing them. Label smoothing is a different intervention.
The temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels; no relevant training trajectories are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The 20% condition replaces labels uniformly, so some replacements retain the original class. The α sweep changes smoothing strength, not corruption rate. Low training accuracy at the reported endpoint does not establish a limit on eventual memorization capacity. This study is not an original source for the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison and convergence as corruption fraction changes.
Shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Only 20% symmetric label noise is tested; no sweep from none to all corruption, and no demonstration that training-set fit remains perfect across that sweep.
The paper does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
No training-time analysis comparing when real patterns and noisy or random labels are learned.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise, without label smoothing (α = 0.0).
rows.measure: Accuracy on the noisy portion of the training set, against the observed noisy labels.
rows.note: Table 3 also reports accuracy against the true labels; the observed-label accuracy is well below perfect.
rows.check: The value is correct: 17.88% accuracy on observed noisy labels shows incomplete fitting after the specified 64,000-step training schedule. It does not establish inability to fit with further training.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise and label smoothing α = 0.1.
rows.measure: Accuracy on the noisy portion of the training set, against the observed noisy labels.
rows.note: The paper says accuracy on the noisy labels decreases as α increases.
rows.check: The value and baseline are correct. Observed noisy-label accuracy is 12.27% with label smoothing; fitting is far from perfect.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise and label smoothing α = 0.2.
rows.measure: Accuracy on the noisy portion of the training set, against the observed noisy labels.
rows.note: The paper says accuracy on the noisy labels decreases as α increases.
rows.check: The value and baseline are correct. Observed noisy-label accuracy is 8.32% with label smoothing; fitting is far from perfect.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise, without label smoothing (α = 0.0).
rows.measure: Accuracy on the noisy portion of the training set, against the true labels.
rows.note: This is accuracy against true labels, so it does not directly measure fitting the observed noisy labels.
rows.check: Accuracy against the original true labels measures recovery of underlying classes, not fitting observed corrupted labels or degradation across corruption rates.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise and label smoothing α = 0.1.
rows.measure: Accuracy on the noisy portion of the training set, against the true labels.
rows.note: This is accuracy against true labels, so it does not directly measure fitting the observed noisy labels.
rows.check: The improvement against true labels measures denoising as smoothing changes, not the noise-rate dependence or memorization named in V4.

relationships.condition: ResNet-32 on CIFAR-100 with 20% uniform label replacement, no label smoothing, after 64,000 training steps
relationships.reason: R1 reports only 17.88% accuracy against observed labels on the corrupted subset, showing incomplete memorization under this training protocol rather than perfect training fit.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy against supplied labels on the corrupted subset reached only 17.88%.

relationships.condition: The same setting with label smoothing α = 0.1 or 0.2
relationships.reason: R2 and R3 report corrupted-subset observed-label accuracies of 12.27% and 8.32%; smoothing further reduces fitting under the tested protocol.
relationships.display_finding: Corrupted-subset accuracy against supplied labels fell to 12.27% and 8.32% with smoothing strengths 0.1 and 0.2, respectively.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-32 on CIFAR-100 with 20% symmetric label noise
reader_labels.reason: The observed noisy-label accuracy is 17.88 without smoothing and falls to 12.27 and 8.32 with smoothing, so the reported results do not show perfect training fit in these conditions (R1–R3). The paper tests no corruption-rate sweep.
